headline: Milling Toward a Climate‑Smaller Port – Experts voice growing anxiety for regional docks
content: **MILLING TOWARD AN CLIMATE‑SMALLER PORT – EXPERTS VOICE GROWING ANXIETY FOR REGIONAL DOCKS** *By Amanda Clarke, Senior Reporter* Port Albert (26 Aug 20XX): With each grain-sheaped wave that kisses the sands off Port Augusta today, one local debate swells faster — the pace and impact of Port Albert’s proposed shift to high‑energy, climate‑optimised freight services, part and parcel of SouthAustralia’s “Sail‑Secure” transport roadmap rolled out last weekend. While municipal leadership cheers this upgrade, a clutch of experts warns that the economic surge could grind slower, smaller cargo fleets straight along the region’s shore‑ejected corridors… “It's less, not more!” --- #### • The Proposed ‘Smaller’ Port? What It Means in Concrete Terms Government releases speak vaguely over technical jargon about an **improved dock system that ‘uses energy more optimally so each cargo movement produces zero excess emissions’.** The actual result is a leaner rail and bulk haul strategy with longer vessel runs, fewer truck‑hauliers along the BHP rail, a focus on carbon‑clean fuel for rail engines and solar power stations straddling the wharf floor. Slight but steady, the changes intend to limit traffic to: * **Upgarde the “Big” port cranes so weight-shifting is maximised at a lean cost of twenty‑odd ton loads; * Install photovoltaic canopies on rail yard parking; * Retrofit diesel freight rail to green electrics;   All as part of the “Green Tugs and Paddrellas Initiative”. The projected carbon offset has been **couched at some $2M annual reduction in local emissions** --- #### • The “Jettisoned Barge? A Furtic of Local Trade Impact” “We expect, simply with rational economics at one level, a shift for long‑haul to shift heavier containers that feed inland communities, with truck routes dwindled to local haul in the new infrastructure and, to emphasise – no long haul trains on short turn‑times across town” (Dr Jamil Noor, *Local Business Analyst*) But as noted before, small “shuttles’ such as local cargo for retail, fisheries and community supplies suffer because freight will funnel to larger scale shipping lanes on long runs. Port Authority head Tom Wilkinson pointed to the “**critical balance will still exist**”—but added a sense of anxious optimism *"We have seen in early feasibility modeling where local firms (both agricultural produce farms here along Gawler and some micro-factories in Adelaide Airport, Port) get their transport costs to run near zero… that it's likely a net *benefit to the overall infrastructure footprint.*" --- ####• Data Matters: Small Businesses – "Where Amid Our Ships, Will Grow, the Liminality Will Fade to the Hallowed Quiet?? “ “They can produce but not deliver.” During interview with *Ellen White*, a local fisher on St Barbo, **concise data reveals: *– in February 12 port 42 out of the monthly fifty “shoppers” of port services have had to leave to avoid shipping or waiting."** In addition, port capacity reduction from moving from bulk cargo to streamlined, heavy ship-lauled freight translates (a port analyst’s guess: **≈15 %—at our low scale—the potential for extra hours in loading and discharge.**) *Therefore some commercial “boats and goods would experience a drop… from four to seven days' wait times”* “The difference with our trade logistics? content: **The Port Augusta Times** 10 December 2025 **School principal declares "Time‑dilatative classroom hours could reinvent learning patterns"** _Inside headlines for Port’s top schools_ By A. Jenkins | Education Correspondent --- When you heard about it, the story sounded straight out of sci‑fi, that the teachers were *rewindingtime* by making lessons stick, longer with new tech. It feels more the flavour of a science-fiction documentary than education conference notes though – “time dilates.” Yet here we are in Parkview Drive, reading about Wyraman Public's experimental idea to *rewindle our day,* stretching the pace of lectures so that what the children do on each 4‑m teaching chunk looks slower to them if only for an experience in the *learning psychology team* has been the ultimate aim. For this we brought a record straight look – or an extended transcript so they don't turn it – straight from Principal Andrew Bury’s front room. “So imagine someone looking at time through time‑dilation glasses from inside the same bubble of the entire unit.” Principal Andrew Bury (Mr B.) [image on side with him in action in the laboratory] "It’s an entirely internal, practical approach within normal schooling regulations.” Mr Bury explains his thinking is 'we keep clocks and budgets right here in normal time yet create *local experience spaces* that are long… slower and at‑less. That's how kids can absorb content, practice in repeated small groups and maintain mental freshness over each cycle". In the pilot on Friday's fourth of that subject cycle last week he installed digital timenarrow tech onto “the entire class cycle," said the headteacher because it's “no science fair in high-school, but a regular 'timetime' experiment as a part of normal syllabus." **Teachers Speak** "Time slowing? Port Augusta Senior Schools Get Early‑Award From Education SA For Climate‑Conscious Curriculum
content: **The Port Augusta Times** 7 Nov 2024 ***Port Augusta Senior Schools Get Early‑Award From Education SA For Climate‑Conscious Curriculum*** Port. This dawn will not only mark another season of sunburnt heat but also another triumphant stride for our own children– an earlier reward for the Port Augusta Secondary educational precincts. Teachers and pupils from the Peninsula North & North Adelaide Schools received an early accreditation award from the Government of South—Education Department for successfully meeting the new State Benchmark for incorporating climate‑focused STEM (C‑STEM) and community response into primary curriculum planning by mid‑October. Why ‘early‐award’? Because the Education Ministers want every senior local teacher to see a certification within one year rather then five to qualify, and the schools submitted a joint plan already and were recognised the past evening (20 Nov during lunch service near the Harbourview complex) as the first North–East coastal region. **Rising stars** – “After six seasons’ training,” Dr. Elaine‑Nol, principal for Al Jungar‑Port Aug: "we felt we simply couldn’t be satisfied with just making changes, only an award will cement the progress." Curric plan includes a three‑hour series: “Ocean – Ecosystem Dynamics”; “Urban Green‑Footprints; ” and a full community garden design in School Hallways & local council‑funded rooftop compost units with ‘Solar panel‑Powered Heat‑to‑Gum‑Charger’. Education Commissioner Matthew Benn’s comment about the early award was “These students and teachers are a shining testifier. For some our entire city would rather stay on a stable old platform; I truly respect those pushing for the first local green curriculum." The curriculum plan will continue to receive a funding push. The school community gave evidence to support the policy decision behind the early acknowledgement by a petition containing thirty local names that are signed by parents, business and government officials with small coffee stalls across South‑Artes. They said climate is here – just as local storms. We can only adapt to make our community safe by putting lessons about sustainable water in. "Everyone that visits these Schools knows they are actively dealing with the planet– in a practical hands-on manner," explains School Senior Adviser Mark Forde to the public for “The Daily Port”, "we teach our kids not always to survive the changing climate‐but also the how to sustain the next step for community". We now stand at early 2055‑10 that is already an important milestone. These early award points, “Punctuate our local leadership at education and local government when it’s concerning sustainable action that matters. PRA’s final release continues a call for “all the state students’ will now know climate in a fun & real approach. There’ll a ‘rewards for those with an excellent demonstration plan’, but we remain, proudly waiting for more local achievements. © The Port Aug, Time‑News ©. (The story continues with the community‑approved, small 12‑hour “Water and Solar” demonstration that has an eco‑design stage, to be opened Friday evening on Sunday to celebrate, plus a ‘plant‑on‑an‑australia event that uses recycled glass, 2mm wood with a fresh and colourful theme ‘Climate – Education. That is what your paper will report for next week) ***For a preview or update feel free, contact TAT – Editor. This news to continue to support climate educational local stories.***

headline: Council Rides on a 'Zero‑DEBT' Commitment for Port Augusta Public Schools
content: **The Port Augusta Times** *City & suburbs • Tuesday 13 January 2024 by: Aunty Jann* --- **Council Rides on a ’Zero‑Debt’ Commitment for Port Augusta Public Schools** A formal declaration entered the municipal clerk’s rolls this week in an attempt to reassure residents that educational expenditure should not burden taxpayers during the next eight years. Mayor Laura Ng Suh, sitting beneath Port Augusta High Street and flattered eyes over the city hall dais on Wednesday dawn, told reporters that the $1 5m per annum annual council levy will support **"a Zero Debt pathway" for every local public junior — senior college under council control."** “Kids are paying on the next generation of jobs, not on legacy budgets," Ms S’s emphatic slogan hammered at an event attended by two hundred school children’s carers and headmasters John Barham from Augusta Primary, Hannah Doherty at Port Alderson School. Council members will keep debts zeroed via an **allocation method where any residual levied revenue will be used immediately, leaving no ‘cousin funds’ open for later years where taxpayers take on more debt**. The measure will, as declared, see a direct lift, "Zero Debt, More Cash," to classrooms to fund teacher salary premiums in next round at +14% — the most dramatic across council-managed, and not funded by State contributions. ### Heads across schools Hugh McGon‑Hunt – Principal Port’s **Port Alderson Public College** wrote a letter to local community, echoing the sentiment that “this Council promise will, according to research & my 12-year audit oversight in Australian federal policy frameworks, ensure no longer-than a month budget debt, thereby strengthening the safety net of students' education quality.” She added concern: “There isn’t enough funding transparency though we cannot deny this is good enough policy on time until $15m for the schools. We see a 75% reduction expected in debt and the 3 per mil growth to next academic fiscal timeline” In reply, the school board and PTA in **East Port Augusta Primary School** are working on extra resources, hoping zero‑debt might let $500, the same sum once earmarked for repairs from building 1967 now move free 200 per cent of capital spending over to actual training. Their teachers also “hopes that there will remain flexibility to upgrade high performance for staff.” ### Opposition notes While teachers applaud the strategy to keep schools under debt, some community advocacy, particularly from senior citizen club "Golden‑Years", say there's not yet detailed accounting on cash buffer, calling this still "policy" "but a financial approach with ‘zero debt” risk. "It sounds nice on paper and may deliver real benefit – but what in it is truly needed that we can watch for?" warns Mark Phillips CEO “Northern Schools Improvement Partners.” Counsillor Tim White also expressed a degree of warning at his position paper on "debt transparency requirements" > “That a simple 70-year period might leave open ‘unexpected growth rates and revenue dips if future schools might have capital projects that do require credit. In these high-savings models our key interest needs to monitor 'not the zero but actual growth', else the board might appear not that transparent or, if miscalculated, this will still fall for debt later" – concluded by a subtle apology of their office on 'no-press, no-debt – so the rest of us will learn to get with them. --- **On our pages** > All details: 9 15am — City council public discussion 10 0 pm – 6am community fundraising > This 5th Street line — our 'Council Minutes', a full PDF attached on *e-campaign. In that part; any other concerns from other voices; look to a future: *if you might help them do this "Zero DEBT," look online about it – it's available soon - * in a few weeks of the full city roll and an immediate announcement of *2025 school improvements as we continue to keep all 6 primary schools at hand. We will still come over 30 million to meet our state obligations, so we stay under a pledge. A small portion is part; they say it can create 20/23% improvement in class‑size while boosting community and workforce. We look forward a "future is ours": – all we can wait for more school funding by that new method or not yet. ---

headline: Environmental Ward Introduces 40‑metre Seclusion Corridor for Riverbank
content: **Environmental Ward Introduces 40‑metre Seclusion Corridor for Riverbank** *New buffer aims to protect native species and improve water quality* Port Augusta, 6 December 2025 – In a move that many eco‑advocates say will give the riverbank a much‑needed breathing space, the City of Port Augusta’s Environmental Ward unveiled plans to create a 40‑metre “seclusion corridor” along the eastern bank of the River Murray. The corridor, fully developed by the autumn, will be a vegetated buffer zone designed to separate recreational land‑use from the sensitive riparian ecosystem, an effort that local wildlife groups say could make a big difference for native birds, fish and other flora. ### “A quiet refuge for our river” Council Environmental Officer, Sarah Hughes, explained the corridor’s purpose to the 90‑person audience that gathered at the Pump Station Community Hall for the announcement. “We’ve got to give the riverbank its own quiet corner,” Hughes told the press. “The seclusion corridor will use native plantings—gum‑tree seedlings, river bottlebrush and some shoreline grass—to create a natural buffer around 40 metres. That buffer will reduce the human footprint, curb erosion and give native wildlife a private space to thrive.” Hughes added that the very term “seclusion” is an intentional nod to the corridor’s role as a sanctuary for the animals that rely on the riverbank. “They’re acting as a corridor, not a barrier,” she emphasized. “They’ll ‘seclude’ the wildlife from the surf‑and‑sand spots where people picnic and cycle, which is especially important when we’re dealing with sensitive species such as the endangered Murray cod and the crab‑claw.” ### Local community takes note The proposal has already attracted voices from both sides of the now‑well‑paddled riverbank trail. Treaty Council member Brendan Austin, who sits on the Planning and Environment Committee, praised the initiative. “If we are serious about protecting our river, it’s a good step,” Austin said. “People will still enjoy the walk or the bike path, but the 40‑metre strip will keep the wildlife in their natural habitat and protect the water quality. That’s a win for the whole community.” Others, however, worry that the new buffer will limit public access to the scenic riverbank. “I love walking at sunrise behind the park,” said 65‑year‑old resident, Hilda Sellers. “I’m a little disappointed the area will be off‑limits. But if it helps the fish that are so important to Port’s fishing tradition, maybe it’ll be worth it.” Council spokesperson, Anna Peters, conceded that the proposal will shift a few popular picnic spots but insisted the overall arrangement would still permit public use. “We are opening a new lookout platform, and the pedestrian path will be widened to accommodate more foot traffic,” Peters said. “The corridor is a look‑ahead measure; it’s not cutting off the river.” ### Legal and environmental backdrop The 40‑metre seclusion corridor sits within a broader compliance framework tied to the *Aquatic Ecosystems Protection Act 2014* and the *Murray‑Darling Basin Plan.* Under those regimes, councils must provide “buffer zones” that support “water‑quality monitoring” and “habitat connectivity.” The corridor will meet the Ministry’s requirement for a 30‑metre buffer and falls well below the maximum 50 metre safe zone prescribed for high‑risk activities. “The Murray‑Darling Basin Plan has been demanding stronger riparian protection, and we’re happy to be ahead of the curve,” said BASA (Bureau of Aquatic Science and Assessment) Director, Dr. Alan Rees. “This corridor is planned to incorporate a riparian planting scheme that will out‑grow currently exposed concrete slopes. The resulting vegetation and some leaf litter will break down, enriching the soil and providing natural filtration for the riverine water.” ### Implementation and timeline According to the Environmental Ward, the corridor’s planting schedule begins late October, with full establishment expected by late March 2026. It will coincidentally align with the time of year when local anglers most frequently harvest Murray cod, giving the fish a protected head start before the peak breeding season. Council officials say community involvement will remain a priority. “We’re launching a volunteer planting program next week,” stated Hughes. “Universities are also coming on board with environmental science students—an opportunity for hands‑on learning and adding credibility to our environmental stewardship.” ### Final thoughts The Environmental Ward’s initiative is seen by many as a bold step toward preserving the unique biodiversity that the River Murray supports in Port Augusta and beyond. Whether it will sprint past the eco‑inequality that sometimes mars urban conservation projects remains to be seen, but the calm, 40‑metre corridor promises to be a quiet haven for wildlife—perhaps just what the river has been craving in the heartbeat of a growing city.

headline: Small-town Heritage Day Turns Into Tax Question That Hits Low Income Housing Support Funding; Some Residents Worsted
content: **The Port Augusta Times** **Small‑town Heritage DayTurns Into Tax Question That Hunts Low Income Housing Funding ** *“Worsented” in community circles as debate sways* October 17, 24 — Residents and visitors took centre‑stage at the third‑year Port Augusta Community Heritage Festival, a long‑standing summer showcase meant to give tourists glimpses of the town’s unique stories. The one‑four‑day celebration opened on a sunny Sunday, featuring market stalls of bush leather art, native garden walks and speeches from longtime community voices. But toward Sunday’s “Local Crafts” parade the day shifted. As local produce stalls finished on a heavy cart of pumpkins—just in time to light lanterns in the main street—voices turned as the crowd’s energy waned to something much different – an all‑important headline about an upcoming tax law in the Legislative Assembly. The matter? An unexpectedly strong State‑government levy that, via an earmark reversal, will slash $2500 k in annual support from the province’s Low‑Income Housing Fund that feeds subsidised rentals across Port Adelaide. It wasn’t clear exactly how the cut would be carried into port. One estimate (not yet vetted by Council auditors) predicted the levy would strip half a percentage point in the tax of rental income tax on all private developments. On the town's 30th main street line‑of-lorry from the heritage walk, Councillors stood on the footpath and explained the law’s purpose. > ***Council Lead Phil Carrow says** “—they hope this increase generates enough revenue to fund heritage festivals from *today’s budget*, but a short fall now for our housing board means rent hikes can reach the lowest earnest of our suburbs.* Many locals heard their hopes evaporate there. Former community hall manager Lily Jones says: “Before there was money and now, how are homes left alone?” On Wednesday council members announced the move from a routine annual town review to a meeting dedicated to how a change of money funding would leave many families looking into alternative “unstructured” accommodations. “We need some new ideas.” Several community pillars who raised local business grants in the last few summer’s events (copper and wool, local music projects in the church hall and the newly‑renormalized open–air markets for locally grown tomatoes in old storage cells ) signaled concern in public meeting. Many turned into small “murmur clusters” that will take effect next February and possibly force residents reliant for monthly subsidies who can only hold the low rates to change their finances that summer months (they fear high cost of living.) “We’ll be sure it stops at no major tax‑question’s loss,*” warned John Allen. “For now they seem to focus our best‑investment on heritage’s new brand – just keep these lines out and leave all the rest to government and our town people.” But how many? For now an analysis remains a rumor (the council isn’s told how large a cut in the funding). Many say only half a portion is affected, “We’ll see next season” according to Tom. He expects some members of the low household rates (including those from “Shire Hall at the community centre”) keep them away for their family. Because there are 4 thousand houses registered by community for the Port- Adelaide town; one in thirty remains a key contributor for small incomes, they feel that if taxes keep being lowered out they’ll fall. “Do the funds have to be split further,” asked Linda? He might still come around. --- ### Bottom line Local politicians and residents hold this year over the new tax change. Council’s role lies in providing more than funding; it should keep those housing that do depend on a supportive state as steady in community support funding of affordable housing even in Port- and Adelaide to keep the public confidence and quality in living. With people left “some a worstered” many look back, there’s a serious conversation to set aside more financial aid with public accountability than a “heritage tourism event”. They will hold discussion until April where council will pass the relevant legislation as necessary.

headline: City Planning Review Supports Future Railway Overpass Upgrader–'Port Augusta–The Route is Safe,' Statement from Office
content: **The Port Augusta Times** *(Port Augusta 2025-12-04 – 11:05 am)* **City Planning Review Supports Future Railway Overpass Upgrad** – 'Port Aug­usta–The Route Is Safe,' Statement from Office Port Augusta officials are giving the green‑light today for a state‑scale road/overpass upgrade above a busy South Australian Railway section. While the city planning office originally earmarked a traffic underpass scheme for three years this decade, recent expert advice indicated significant construction benefits associated simply lifting all through‑traffic above the track—leading a council sub‑commission to recommend a fixed‑grade “overtrack” upgrade and full‑time rail security. According to “Plan” Senior Adviser Rebecca Lane and her Urban Mobility team. “We reviewed a battery of projects, considering peak commuter‑flow estimates, vehicular safety studies issued at Perth, local ecological surveys and federal budget provisions,” she told the staff media meeting yesterday. The revised Plan states there remains no plan “in public debate stage— we only put them there because it will need high level cross‑government endorsement." --- ### Safety, Capacity The City‑Spedway Review A major 2024‑24 City Plan for Port Aug-aug's growth sees increased population near Route 29 heading in with daily commutes via Cal Road; thus state ministers for Transport were told that even modest “tactical” overbridg‑ upgrades reduce both accidents rates by‑5 to 6 ppm (perth traffic modelling predicts from the original $4½×3 Mm undertrack). *By Jane Porter, Community Correspondent*

In this week's local column we turn a spotlight on Mr. Darren Cole, a 39‑year‑old resident whose fresh focus on volunteerism is already energizing the Port Augusta community.

## From Corporate Boardrooms to Coffee‑shop Coffee Roasters

For the past decade, Cole spent his career leading project‑teams for a Fortune‑500 tech company in Adelaide. After retiring from the position of Senior Project Manager—thanks in part to a generous early‑pension scheme—he bought a modest, one‑story plant in a busy coffee roaster’s shop. Where the shop’s coffee scent hangs heavily over tables, visitors encounter more than beans and latte art; they’ll find one of Port Augusta's biggest benefactors helping in community spaces.

> "It seemed almost impossible that after fifteen years in technology I could turn back the clock in my own neighbourhood. That notion is exactly what drew me," said Cole.

headline: City Council Unveils New Development at Port Swale
content:
**Port Augusta, November 9, 2025** – In a press release this week, Mayor Susan Blake opened plans to transform

Port Swale from a historic working harbor into a mixed‑use gateway, fusing residential luxury with recreational shipping. The city’s Vision 2040 blueprint has identified “creative adaptation on soft terrain” in this maritime neighbourhood

---

**Historic Roots Meeting Modern Growth**

Port Swale, so far known for tug‑boats servicing north‑regional freight routes, receives the official endorsement for mixed development on the 82‑acre stretch flagged under Town/8 Opinion. While some long‑time yacht harbours residents are wary about heavier commercial influx, “growth and adaptation with respect for the past keep the area vibrant’’ Mayor Blake explained during council meetings Saturday evening.

---

**What Residents Can Expect**

* Residential “low‑rise water‑oriented loft community” (12 plots, ~450 applied acres).

* Parkland extension that promotes safe paths to swale and lagoon in an added 41 ha shoreline conservation board at Riverbend Reserve (link–park-map).

* Heritage‑stressing shipping routes re‑furnished by steel cables (a "classic design meets coastal eco‑modern") replacing the port barge docking for five centuries.

---

**City Economic and Social Predictions**

Pre-construction demand for workforce grew fast from a previous 20% under municipal labour growth targets. With an estimated budget of $73 mln forecast for Phase 1, The Port Augusta Planning Department quoted: "While this phase delivers essential job placements, the public transportation backbone is being retro-rated prior to expansion to maintain commute time below 11 minute," noted infrastructure engineer Carla Valdez.

The development plan comes with an integrated civic kitchen opening plan "Community kitchen concept 2027: >0 community‑based cuisine programs featuring low‑permanent feed in kitchen’s lower hull kitchen."

-----------

**Stakeholder Insights**

Interviewed senior conservation activist Joel Mills of the Heritage Save Project wrote "Preserve historic maritime integrity while integrating sustainable spaces must follow at the harbour edge for resilient future tourism 2‑D and climate resilience. headline: Lily Collins Sparks a Health Revival in Port Augusta
content:
*Port Augusta Times – 6 December 2025*

---

## The story behind Lily Collins

Local resident Lily Collins has made headlines this month after unveiling the **“Healthy Horizons”** program in partnership with Port Augusta Health Services. The initiative, aimed at boosting community wellness, offers free fitness classes, nutrition workshops, and mental‑health seminars—free to all residents.

### Why Lily matters

- **Community first:** Lily, 32, has been a volunteer for the Port Augusta Food Bank for six years.

- **Health champion:** She holds a Bachelor’s in Public Health and a certification in holistic nutrition.

- **Personal drive:** After her own family member endured a heart‑attack, Lily said, “I wanted to give back and help others prevent it.”

### Program details

| Activity | Frequency | Location | Cost |

|----------|-----------|----------|------|

| **Morning Yoga** | Mon–Fri, 6 am | City Park, north side | Free |

| **Nutrition Workshop** | First Saturday of each month | City Hall, #3 |

| **Mental‑Health Talk** | Second Thursday of each month | Community Centre, #1 | Free |

Lily’s team is also launching a **“Wellness Walk”** trail app, making fitness data easily shareable among community members.

### Community response

– *“Finally, a program that cares about our whole well‑being,”* says 45‑year‑old shopkeeper Rajeev Patel.

– The Port Augusta City Council has pledged $50,000 in support to keep the program running for at least two years.

### How to join

Participants can register online at **portaugusta.health/healthyhorizons** or call the Health Services hotline at 0800 PA‑HEAL.

---

**Related article:** For more on health initiatives in Port Augusta, check out our 7_health section.

headline: Bridge Back to Health: The Old Bridge Revitalizes Community Well‑Being
content:
*The Port Augusta Times – Health & Lifestyle Section*

---

The historic **Old Bridge** that once carried cars and trams across the River Torrens is undergoing a transformation that could change the way residents of Port Augusta experience health and mobility. What started as a preservation effort is now a wellness initiative designed to encourage walking, cycling, and social connection in the heart of the city.

## From Iron to Inspiration

Built in 1863, the Old Bridge is one of the oldest surviving structures in the region. For over a century it served as the main traffic artery, but by the late 20th‑century the rise of automobiles and changes in river traffic rendered its road deck obsolete. In 2005 a heritage council listing preserved the bridge, and since then it has lain dormant for almost two decades—until the city council and local health authorities decided that this piece of history could also be a tool for better public health.

> *“Reopening the bridge is not just about keeping our heritage alive,”* says Dr. Emily Ross, spokesperson for the Port Augusta Health Department. *“It’s about creating a safe, accessible place where people can walk, cycle, and meet each other in a healthy environment.”*

## Health Benefits of Bridge Re‑opening

The bridge’s new purpose goes far beyond tourism. The health department’s latest study estimates that a 100‑meter bike‑path can reduce residents’ daily commute time by an average of 5 minutes, leading to measurable boosts in physical activity. Recent data from the council’s community health monitoring project indicates:

- **+12%** increase in walking and cycling among local 18‑to‑34 year olds

- **+8%** decrease in reported mental‑health stress scores in the surrounding neighborhoods

- **+5%** rise in local use of the park space featured on the bridge’s northern end

These numbers reflect the bridge’s dual role as both a *mountain of history* and *a city of wellness*—an inspiring example of urban planning that respects the past while moving forward.

## Community Programs on the Bridge

To maximize the bridge’s impact and keep its visitors safe, the following programs have been launched:

| Program | Frequency | Details |

|--------|-----------|---------|

| **Morning Walks** | Daily | 6 am‑7 am guided walks, led by local fitness trainers. |

| **Wheelchair Accessible Path** | Every Saturday | Dedicated path with step‑free entry, open for senior citizens. |

| **Bike‑Swap Nights** | First Friday of each month | Free bike repair and swap station, with volunteers from the Park Rangers group. |

| **Bridge Café** | Open 8 am‑6 pm | Café offering locally sourced produce, a healthy coffee subscription option, and a Wi‑Fi station for remote workers. |

These initiatives have already attracted a wave of new visitors—especially families with children and retirees—creating a vibrant, inclusive atmosphere on the bridge.

## Economic and Environmental Upside

Local business owner Ravi Patel says the Old Bridge has breathed new life into the town center. “We’ve seen a 20% rise in foot traffic to the cafés and shops along the riverside,” he remarks. “People coming to stroll or cycle on the bridge bring with them lunch, vibe, and ultimately new customers.”

From an environmental standpoint, the bridge’s pedestrian and cycle-only policy reduces car use in the most congested part of town. The *Port Augusta Port Authority* estimates a net reduction in CO₂ emissions of roughly 1,400 kg per week—an impressive figure for any small city.

## How to Get Involved

Citizens interested in participating can sign up for the monthly volunteer coordinator’s list on the city’s website, or pick up a volunteer registration form at the bridge’s information desk during the program times listed above. Donations—whether in cash or in-kind—are also welcomed by the Old Bridge Community Trust.

content:
**Port Augusta** – The *Port Augusta Times* has unveiled its new Sunday edition today, promising readers a fresh weekend perspective that highlights local stories, community events and in‑depth reporting on municipal affairs.

## Why a Sunday Paper?

- **Greater reach:** Sunday circulation is typically higher in regional areas, giving residents more time to digest detailed stories.

- **Local government spotlight:** The new edition will feature a dedicated *Local Government* section, covering council meetings, development plans and community consultations.

- **Feature pieces:** From profile portraits of long‑standing council members to investigative pieces on planning proposals, the Sunday paper will provide comprehensive content that aligns with the needs of the Port Augusta community.

## Featured Articles in the Debut Issue

- **“Council’s New Housing Initiative: What It Means for Port Augusta”** – an analysis of the upcoming development strategy proposed by the local council.

- **“Interview with Mayor Jane Robinson”** – a conversation about the township’s future vision.

- **“Community Voices: How Residents are Shaping Tomorrow”** – a collection of letters and op‑eds from local residents.

*The Sunday edition will also include a calendar of upcoming public consultations, a gardening tips corridor for the suburban neighbourhoods, and a culinary column featuring the region’s best eateries.*

> “We’re excited to offer a Sunday paper that not only informs but also empowers our community by spotlighting the local government's work,” says Editor‑in‑Chief, Alex Thompson.

The new Sunday issue will be available at all Port Augusta Times newsstands from 9 a.m. onwards, and can also be accessed digitally through the Times website or the *Port Augusta Times* app.

**For more information, visit the local government section of the Times website under “1_local_government.”**

headline: New Health Board to Oversee Port Augusta Health Services
content:
*Published in The Port Augusta Times – Local Government Section*

---

The Port Augusta City Council today announced the formation of a **New Health Board** that will take over oversight of the region’s public health facilities. The board will replace the former Medical Board with a more community‑focused approach aimed at improving accessibility, transparency, and funding efficiency across the council area.

### Who’s on the Board?

- **Dr. Elaine Robinson** – Chair (Port Augusta General Hospital Director)

- **Mark Patel** – Deputy Chair (Civic Health Officer)

- **Julie Houghton** – Community Health Specialist

- **Tom Chen** – Health Finance Analyst (Unincorporated)

- **Linda Smith** – Representative of the Local Council

*All members are appointed by City Council, subject to public consultation.*

### What Will the Board Do?

- **Strategic Planning** – Develop a 5‑year health services plan for Port Augusta and surrounding towns.

- **Budget Oversight** – Monitor and approve an annual health budget of $48 million, ensuring funds are directed toward priority services such as chronic disease management and rural outreach.

- **Quality Assurance** – Set performance metrics for hospitals, clinics, and community health programs; publish quarterly reports.

- **Community Engagement** – Host monthly town‑hall meetings and online forums to gather feedback from residents and health professionals.

### Why a New Board?

Previous reviews highlighted gaps in coordination between local health providers and the council. The new board seeks to:

- **Improve Health Outcomes** – Through focused investment in preventative care and early intervention.

- **Increase Transparency** – With monthly public reports and open data dashboards.

- **Enhance Accountability** – By linking funding decisions directly to measurable health indicators.

### Local Government Context

This announcement comes as part of a broader review by the **1_local_government** department to streamline service delivery across the region. The port city’s *Local Government Section* will continue to monitor the board’s performance closely and publish regular updates.

---

**Contact:**

The Port Augusta Times Health Desk – email health@portaugusta.com.

**Next Issue:** Expected to include the first quarterly report from the new Health Board.

Port Augusta’s **Public Services Headquarters** coordinates road and airport staff resources across the state, yet in terms of transportation, this office merges municipal bureaucracy straight into commuters’ planning networks for up‑wind routes and services like Bus lines 1105 A/M (Port‑Centre), Trail routes N5/B and, at daylight, contracted on‑demand Klook Express vans from the Northern and Pacific hubs.

**Practical Benefits & Numbers:**

1. **90 % efficiency hike** after streamlining bus dispatch from the Admin suite & new integrated‑signboards.

2. Average waiting–point in Port Augusta is reduced `+25 minutes`.

3—**24/7 service** for emergency communications across airport and private ports.

At a listening window on a Wednesday roundtrip survey dated September: 52 % of interview patients on staff who responded reported finding buses closer as under­stand before moving to Office HQ. Those at‑home members answered the road link line by 19 h quicker after implementing the system on **Friday**.

Some new feature under current jurisdiction: 5‑step verification required, giving the next set of officers more *full access after three days* that last round. (You know it's done if a sign says "Official Staff – verified”)

**Going forward** more synergy could reach both bus and track. Our department plans road overlays linking transport lanes to adjacent office sublines that enable municipal or tourism visits into the park district earlier in mornings.

headline: **# Lifestyle Correspondency: Friends Circle Builds a New Community Hub**
content:
*Port Augusta, 6 August 2025* – A group of volunteers and local businesses has come together under the banner of **Lifestyle Correspondency** to construct a fresh community center in the heart of Port Augusta. The project, dubbed **Friends Circle Builds**, began in March and is slated for completion next month, providing residents with a versatile space for events, workshops, and social gatherings.

## What the Project Aims to Achieve

- **Reclaiming unused land** – The center is built on a former parking lot that had lain vacant for over a decade.

- **Promoting community cohesion** – Regular meetings, fitness classes, and art‑therapy sessions will be offered to all age groups.

- **Sustainable construction** – Green roofs, solar panels, and recycled building materials were selected to reduce the building’s carbon footprint.

> “We believe that when people come together, they can transform an ordinary piece of land into something extraordinary,” said **Megan Rhee**, Project Lead and local lifestyle columnist. “This is a tangible manifestation of our community’s spirit.”

## Key Milestones

- **March 2021** – Project launched and community rally held on Main Street.

- **February 2025** – Foundation laid; remote workers collaborated on design via livestream.

- **May 2025** – 80% of construction completed, with a soft opening scheduled for late July.

- **October 2025** – Official grand opening, attended by over 500 residents and local dignitaries.

## Community Involvement

The **Friends Circle Builds** initiative not only provided a physical space but also created numerous volunteer opportunities. 245 residents logged their hours on the construction site, and more than 30 local businesses donated materials or services.

### Success Stories

| Volunteer | Contribution | Comment |

|-----------|--------------|---------|

| Liam Patel | Masonry | “I never thought I’d get to use my skills for a real community project.” |

| Nia Cohen | Interior design | “Seeing the space come together was a gift.” |

| John Martinez | Scriptwriting | “I documented the project, and the footage is now part of the city’s history.” |

## Looking Ahead

The centre will host:

- **Weekly “Queer COVID‑Safe” tea‑times** for the LGBTQ+ community.

- **Monthly “Craft & Coffee” mornings** for local artisans.

- **Year‑round “Lifestyle Correspondency” seminars** that cover topics from mental health to eco‑friendly living.

The building’s opening will further foster the sense of belonging among Port Augusta’s diverse neighborhoods.

> “This is just the beginning,” noted city councilor **Aisha Rahman** during the opening ceremony. “With the Friends Circle Builds, we are nurturing a healthier, more connected Port Augusta.”

---

For more community updates and stories about local projects, visit the **[6_community](#6_community)** section of *The Port Augusta Times*.

headline: Conventional Titan for Peace
content:
**Port Augusta Times**

*Port Augusta, 6 December 2025*

The city of Port Augusta has recently hosted a landmark event dubbed the **Conventional Titan for Peace** convention, bringing together environmental scientists, military strategists, and community leaders to explore how conventional (non‑nuclear) security measures can help prevent conflicts and foster sustainable development.

## A New Approach to Peacekeeping

At the heart of the convention was the discussion of large‑scale **conventional defence systems**—projectiles, drones, and barrier technologies—that, unlike their nuclear counterparts, carry a lower risk of escalation. The slogan “**Conventional Titan for Peace**” emphasised the dual role these systems can play: protecting communities from external threats while reducing the global appetite for nuclear armaments.

**“When we can rely on robust, low‑yield conventional forces, the diplomatic options widen dramatically,”** said Dr. Maya Clarke, a senior researcher at the Australian Defence Research School. **“It gives us a stepping stone to de‑militarise hotspots without compromising safety.”**

## Environmental Co‑Benefits

A key pillar of the convention was the environmental impact of deploying such systems. According to the **Department of Environment, Water, Heritage and the Arts**, conventional defence projects can be designed to minimise ecological footprints by:

- Using local materials to reduce carbon emissions during construction

- Partnering with renewable‑energy companies to power installations

- Implementing smart‑maintenance protocols to extend lifespan and reduce waste

These measures, the department said, align with the city’s larger goal of becoming a **carbon‑neutral hub by 2035**.

## Community‑Led Peace Initiatives

The convention also launched a series of **community‑led “Peace Pods”**—small, community‑managed defence platforms that can be activated in times of crisis. Each pod will be staffed and maintained by volunteers, offering a “human‑facilitated” approach to security that emphasises transparency and accountability.

**“We want peace not only to be a strategy on a charts of war,”** said council member James O’Neill. **“It must be a lived reality for our citizens.”**

## Looking Ahead

The convention concluded with a **Coalition for Conventional Peace** agreement, urging national governments to adopt a framework that prioritises conventional defense tools over nuclear arsenals. The coalition will meet again next year in Adelaide for a review of progress.

As Port Augusta celebrates its growing reputation as an environmental forward‑thinking city, the **Conventional Titan for Peace** initiative stands as a testament to the belief that peace and sustainability can—and must—go hand in hand.

*For further details, visit the city’s official website or contact the Department of Environment’s media office.*

content:
**The Port Augusta Times** – *Public Safety Section (4_public_safety)*

In a developing story that has raised alarms across the region, Senior Superintendent Paul Smith of the Port Augusta Police Service has been named as a suspect in a series of questionable disciplinary actions and alleged misconduct. Investigators are now examining whether his actions may have compromised public safety, prompting a review of the department’s internal oversight procedures.

## Background

- **Position** – Senior Superintendent, Traffic & Community Safety Division

- **Tenure** – Over 12 years in the force, with 6 years as a superintendent

- **Reported Issues** – A series of officer complaints, unexplained disciplinary suspensions, and allegations of improper use of force

### Key Allegations

| Allegation | Details | Current Status |

|------------|---------|----------------|

| **Improper Use of Force** | Multiple reports of excessive force during traffic stops, some leading to injuries. | Investigations underway. |

| **Misallocation of Resources** | Accusations of diverting vehicles and personnel from high‑risk areas for personal use. | Police records cross‑checked; preliminary audit inconclusive. |

| **Failure to Report** | Reports of omitting 16 alleged infractions from official logs. | Police Superior Officers Council reviewing. |

## Impact on Public Safety

The Port Augusta Times has received numerous inquiries from residents concerned that:

- **Risk of Disaster Response** – Mismanagement of critical resources could delay emergency response times during natural or man‑made incidents.

- **Trust in Law Enforcement** – Public confidence in local policing ranks in decline.

- **Officer Morale** – Several junior officers have announced plans to transfer to neighboring districts citing a “turbulent environment.”

## Official Response

The Police Service Business, led by Chief Commissioner Jane Doe, has announced a *“comprehensive, independent review”* to determine the authenticity of the allegations:

1. **Internal Affairs Investigation Team** – Operating in collaboration with the Independent Police Integrity Authority (IPIA).

2. **Transparency Initiative** – Releasing anonymised data on patrol priorities and resource allocation to the public.

3. **Community Liaison** – Scheduling town‑hall meetings to discuss resident concerns and the findings of the investigation.

> **Chief Commissioner Jane Doe**: “Public safety is our foremost duty. We are committed to a thorough, unbiased review that upholds the integrity of our department.”

## What Residents Can Do

- **Report** – Any concerns or witnessed incidents can be filed through the official portaugusta.police.gov.au/complaints portal.

- **Attend Meetings** – The next public safety briefing is scheduled for 12 May 2025 at 7 p.m. in the Civic Hall, City Hall.

- **Stay Informed** – The Port Augusta Times will provide daily updates until the investigation concludes.

---

**Editor's Note:** This article is part of the *4_public_safety* coverage intended to keep the Port Augusta community informed. It remains a developing story; further details will be added as the investigation proceeds.

- **Redevelopment Complete:** Main Street infrastructure is fully finished after a two‑year regeneration package worth $15 million

**HEADLINE:** *Local Pulse – Mayor Stuart Roberts — Navigating Growth While Keeping Community Values Front‑Front*

**By Samantha D’Arcy – 1_local_government Team**

**Port Augusta, AU, 27 September 2025**

---

The heart of Port Augusta’s governance has long been guided by an individual balancing progress with pride in the region’s cultural fabric. This month, the council and the city‑wide readership turn their focus on one figure at the helm: **Mayor Stuart Roberts**.

**Background & Rise**

> • Born and bred in Port Augusta, Stuart took over the mayoral office in 2021 following a council recall.

> • His prior years on the Planning and Services board championed eco‑friendly projects and community engagement.

> • Critics labelled the quick pivot between party platforms as a "crossover compromise".

**Policy Highlights**

1. **Sustainable Growth Agenda**

- “Port Augusta should keep rising while remembering what makes our corner the closest to Earth,” said Roberts.

- The 2022 Plan Green Boost subsidises community gardens, wildlife corridors, and mixed‑use developments.

2. **Port Enhancement for All**

- Miller Landing expansion improved storm‑water flooding tolerance *and* pedestrian lanes for commuters.

3. **Community Cohesion Initiatives**

- Year‑long "Stories at Sundown" programme launched to let town members recount lives that shaped neighbourhood identity.

**Controversies**

| Issue | What It Is | Mayor's Stance | Reaction |

|-------|------------|----------------|----------|

| The Harbor Lane | Contract renew‑al for maintenance crews | ‘Fair terms, timely execution.’ | Local businesses applauding improved schedules |

| Cultural Resource Conservation | Proposed shift in land‑use codes near old mill ruins | ‘Preserve but permit upgrades.’ | Archaeological Society issuing statement |

**Public Perception**

> *“We have this optimistic vibe that was missing before Stuart.”*

> — *May, 21 Atoise Resident, <1‑½ km north of river.*

**Community Testimonies**

- **Amira Al‑Jafari**, environmental NGO:  *“He introduced a real incentive for reforesting.”*

- **Leonardo Schmidt**, chief engineer of local power:  *“Reductions in carbon have translated into smaller utility bills.”*

**Personal Side**

Mayor Stuart is the type who plans “afternoons on the paddle‐board deck for Sunday family outing while sitting on a concrete wall about your ideas.”

**Quote from Mayor**

> *“The horizon can seem as wide as you want but to realize progress lies in each brick of small talk, community meal or a town debate where voices linger into the night.”*

> –  Stuart Roberts

**Upcoming Focus – 2026 Port Augusta Open Planning Summit**

- “Port Augusta values community values while pushing a *path to thrive.”* –  The Council.

- Address for youth representatives will be televised February next year at Miller Landing hall; RSVP needed.

### Contact Information

**Mayor Stuart Roberts**

Attn: City Planning & Development Office

headline: Local Resident Shifts Gears Toward Community Service
content:
*The Port Augusta Times – June 7 , 2025*

*By Jane Porter, Community Correspondent*

---

In this week's local column we turn a spotlight on Mr. Darren Cole, a 39‑year‑old resident whose fresh focus on volunteerism is already energizing the Port Augusta community.

## From Corporate Boardrooms to Coffee‑shop Coffee Roasters

For the past decade, Cole spent his career leading project‑teams for a Fortune‑500 tech company in Adelaide. After retiring from the position of Senior Project Manager—thanks in part to a generous early‑pension scheme—he bought a modest, one‑story plant in a busy coffee roaster’s shop. Where the shop’s coffee scent hangs heavily over tables, visitors encounter more than beans and latte art; they’ll find one of Port Augusta's biggest benefactors helping in community spaces.

> "It seemed almost impossible that after fifteen years in technology I could turn back the clock in my own neighbourhood. That notion is exactly what drew me," said Cole.

*An added bonus: Port Augusta’s social services record higher uptake rates in coffeehouse areas post opening. *

## Daily Habits and Weekly Rituals

**Daily ritual.** The sunrise at 5:35 a.m., while the streets are dim but the roaster's lights burning, inspires Darren with a perspective different from spreadsheets – it feeds an eye for possibilities.

**Weekly routine.** *3 p.m.–6 p.m.* – Coffee coffee times out are scheduled for community outreach with “World Compassion Youth Mission” visits: school‑goer after school teams help handout lunch boxes on busy stretches of Siefert road.

**Social media influence**. There has not been a measurable difference to their recent exposure on Instagram despite a short selfie photo captured by fans on March, when “socially required “by other community citizens, for not sure they’re yet still using marketing” that quickly garnered shares.”

The underlying benefit is at present that Dardan.

**Key takeaways**. *Key* aspects – each factor holds enormous potential:

* Local footstep drive: on par.

* Decreases sense: higher level of pride felt by participants at times when students discuss academic concerns, through consistent volunteers within close working area.

headline: City Council Unveils New Development at Port Swale
content:
**Port Augusta, November 9, 2025** – In a press release this week, Mayor Susan Blake opened plans to transform

Port Swale from a historic working harbor into a mixed‑use gateway, fusing residential luxury with recreational shipping. The city’s Vision 2040 blueprint has identified “creative adaptation on soft terrain” in this maritime neighbourhood

---

**Historic Roots Meeting Modern Growth**

Port Swale, so far known for tug‑boats servicing north‑regional freight routes, receives the official endorsement for mixed development on the 82‑acre stretch flagged under Town/8 Opinion. While some long‑time yacht harbours residents are wary about heavier commercial influx, “growth and adaptation with respect for the past keep the area vibrant’’ Mayor Blake explained during council meetings Saturday evening.

---

**What Residents Can Expect**

* Residential “low‑rise water‑oriented loft community” (12 plots, ~450 applied acres).

* Parkland extension that promotes safe paths to swale and lagoon in an added 41 ha shoreline conservation board at Riverbend Reserve (link–park-map).

* Heritage‑stressing shipping routes re‑furnished by steel cables (a "classic design meets coastal eco‑modern") replacing the port barge docking for five centuries.

---

**City Economic and Social Predictions**

Pre-construction demand for workforce grew fast from a previous 20% under municipal labour growth targets. With an estimated budget of $73 mln forecast for Phase 1, The Port Augusta Planning Department quoted: "While this phase delivers essential job placements, the public transportation backbone is being retro-rated prior to expansion to maintain commute time below 11 minute," noted infrastructure engineer Carla Valdez.

The development plan comes with an integrated civic kitchen opening plan "Community kitchen concept 2027: >0 community‑based cuisine programs featuring low‑permanent feed in kitchen’s lower hull kitchen."

-----------

**Stakeholder Insights**

Interviewed senior conservation activist Joel Mills of the Heritage Save Project wrote "Preserve historic maritime integrity while integrating sustainable spaces must follow at the harbour edge for resilient future tourism 2‑D and climate resilience. headline: Lily Collins Sparks a Health Revival in Port Augusta
content:
*Port Augusta Times – 6 December 2025*

---

## The story behind Lily Collins

Local resident Lily Collins has made headlines this month after unveiling the **“Healthy Horizons”** program in partnership with Port Augusta Health Services. The initiative, aimed at boosting community wellness, offers free fitness classes, nutrition workshops, and mental‑health seminars—free to all residents.

### Why Lily matters

- **Community first:** Lily, 32, has been a volunteer for the Port Augusta Food Bank for six years.

- **Health champion:** She holds a Bachelor’s in Public Health and a certification in holistic nutrition.

- **Personal drive:** After her own family member endured a heart‑attack, Lily said, “I wanted to give back and help others prevent it.”

### Program details

| Activity | Frequency | Location | Cost |

|----------|-----------|----------|------|

| **Morning Yoga** | Mon–Fri, 6 am | City Park, north side | Free |

| **Nutrition Workshop** | First Saturday of each month | City Hall, #3 |

| **Mental‑Health Talk** | Second Thursday of each month | Community Centre, #1 | Free |

Lily’s team is also launching a **“Wellness Walk”** trail app, making fitness data easily shareable among community members.

### Community response

– *“Finally, a program that cares about our whole well‑being,”* says 45‑year‑old shopkeeper Rajeev Patel.

– The Port Augusta City Council has pledged $50,000 in support to keep the program running for at least two years.

### How to join

Participants can register online at **portaugusta.health/healthyhorizons** or call the Health Services hotline at 0800 PA‑HEAL.

---

**Related article:** For more on health initiatives in Port Augusta, check out our 7_health section.

headline: Bridge Back to Health: The Old Bridge Revitalizes Community Well‑Being
content:
*The Port Augusta Times – Health & Lifestyle Section*

---

The historic **Old Bridge** that once carried cars and trams across the River Torrens is undergoing a transformation that could change the way residents of Port Augusta experience health and mobility. What started as a preservation effort is now a wellness initiative designed to encourage walking, cycling, and social connection in the heart of the city.

## From Iron to Inspiration

Built in 1863, the Old Bridge is one of the oldest surviving structures in the region. For over a century it served as the main traffic artery, but by the late 20th‑century the rise of automobiles and changes in river traffic rendered its road deck obsolete. In 2005 a heritage council listing preserved the bridge, and since then it has lain dormant for almost two decades—until the city council and local health authorities decided that this piece of history could also be a tool for better public health.

> *“Reopening the bridge is not just about keeping our heritage alive,”* says Dr. Emily Ross, spokesperson for the Port Augusta Health Department. *“It’s about creating a safe, accessible place where people can walk, cycle, and meet each other in a healthy environment.”*

## Health Benefits of Bridge Re‑opening

The bridge’s new purpose goes far beyond tourism. The health department’s latest study estimates that a 100‑meter bike‑path can reduce residents’ daily commute time by an average of 5 minutes, leading to measurable boosts in physical activity. Recent data from the council’s community health monitoring project indicates:

- **+12%** increase in walking and cycling among local 18‑to‑34 year olds

- **+8%** decrease in reported mental‑health stress scores in the surrounding neighborhoods

- **+5%** rise in local use of the park space featured on the bridge’s northern end

These numbers reflect the bridge’s dual role as both a *mountain of history* and *a city of wellness*—an inspiring example of urban planning that respects the past while moving forward.

## Community Programs on the Bridge

To maximize the bridge’s impact and keep its visitors safe, the following programs have been launched:

| Program | Frequency | Details |

|--------|-----------|---------|

| **Morning Walks** | Daily | 6 am‑7 am guided walks, led by local fitness trainers. |

| **Wheelchair Accessible Path** | Every Saturday | Dedicated path with step‑free entry, open for senior citizens. |

| **Bike‑Swap Nights** | First Friday of each month | Free bike repair and swap station, with volunteers from the Park Rangers group. |

| **Bridge Café** | Open 8 am‑6 pm | Café offering locally sourced produce, a healthy coffee subscription option, and a Wi‑Fi station for remote workers. |

These initiatives have already attracted a wave of new visitors—especially families with children and retirees—creating a vibrant, inclusive atmosphere on the bridge.

## Economic and Environmental Upside

Local business owner Ravi Patel says the Old Bridge has breathed new life into the town center. “We’ve seen a 20% rise in foot traffic to the cafés and shops along the riverside,” he remarks. “People coming to stroll or cycle on the bridge bring with them lunch, vibe, and ultimately new customers.”

From an environmental standpoint, the bridge’s pedestrian and cycle-only policy reduces car use in the most congested part of town. The *Port Augusta Port Authority* estimates a net reduction in CO₂ emissions of roughly 1,400 kg per week—an impressive figure for any small city.

## How to Get Involved

Citizens interested in participating can sign up for the monthly volunteer coordinator’s list on the city’s website, or pick up a volunteer registration form at the bridge’s information desk during the program times listed above. Donations—whether in cash or in-kind—are also welcomed by the Old Bridge Community Trust.

headline: Port Augusta Times Launches Sunday Edition, Expanding Focus on Local Government
content:
**Port Augusta** – The *Port Augusta Times* has unveiled its new Sunday edition today, promising readers a fresh weekend perspective that highlights local stories, community events and in‑depth reporting on municipal affairs.

## Why a Sunday Paper?

- **Greater reach:** Sunday circulation is typically higher in regional areas, giving residents more time to digest detailed stories.

- **Local government spotlight:** The new edition will feature a dedicated *Local Government* section, covering council meetings, development plans and community consultations.

- **Feature pieces:** From profile portraits of long‑standing council members to investigative pieces on planning proposals, the Sunday paper will provide comprehensive content that aligns with the needs of the Port Augusta community.

## Featured Articles in the Debut Issue

- **“Council’s New Housing Initiative: What It Means for Port Augusta”** – an analysis of the upcoming development strategy proposed by the local council.

- **“Interview with Mayor Jane Robinson”** – a conversation about the township’s future vision.

- **“Community Voices: How Residents are Shaping Tomorrow”** – a collection of letters and op‑eds from local residents.

*The Sunday edition will also include a calendar of upcoming public consultations, a gardening tips corridor for the suburban neighbourhoods, and a culinary column featuring the region’s best eateries.*

> “We’re excited to offer a Sunday paper that not only informs but also empowers our community by spotlighting the local government's work,” says Editor‑in‑Chief, Alex Thompson.

The new Sunday issue will be available at all Port Augusta Times newsstands from 9 a.m. onwards, and can also be accessed digitally through the Times website or the *Port Augusta Times* app.

**For more information, visit the local government section of the Times website under “1_local_government.”**

headline: New Health Board to Oversee Port Augusta Health Services
content:
*Published in The Port Augusta Times – Local Government Section*

---

The Port Augusta City Council today announced the formation of a **New Health Board** that will take over oversight of the region’s public health facilities. The board will replace the former Medical Board with a more community‑focused approach aimed at improving accessibility, transparency, and funding efficiency across the council area.

### Who’s on the Board?

- **Dr. Elaine Robinson** – Chair (Port Augusta General Hospital Director)

- **Mark Patel** – Deputy Chair (Civic Health Officer)

- **Julie Houghton** – Community Health Specialist

- **Tom Chen** – Health Finance Analyst (Unincorporated)

- **Linda Smith** – Representative of the Local Council

*All members are appointed by City Council, subject to public consultation.*

### What Will the Board Do?

- **Strategic Planning** – Develop a 5‑year health services plan for Port Augusta and surrounding towns.

- **Budget Oversight** – Monitor and approve an annual health budget of $48 million, ensuring funds are directed toward priority services such as chronic disease management and rural outreach.

- **Quality Assurance** – Set performance metrics for hospitals, clinics, and community health programs; publish quarterly reports.

- **Community Engagement** – Host monthly town‑hall meetings and online forums to gather feedback from residents and health professionals.

### Why a New Board?

Previous reviews highlighted gaps in coordination between local health providers and the council. The new board seeks to:

- **Improve Health Outcomes** – Through focused investment in preventative care and early intervention.

- **Increase Transparency** – With monthly public reports and open data dashboards.

- **Enhance Accountability** – By linking funding decisions directly to measurable health indicators.

### Local Government Context

This announcement comes as part of a broader review by the **1_local_government** department to streamline service delivery across the region. The port city’s *Local Government Section* will continue to monitor the board’s performance closely and publish regular updates.

---

**Contact:**

The Port Augusta Times Health Desk – email health@portaugusta.com.

**Next Issue:** Expected to include the first quarterly report from the new Health Board.

headline: **# Lifestyle Correspondency: Friends Circle Builds a New Community Hub**
content:
*Port Augusta, 6 August 2025* – A group of volunteers and local businesses has come together under the banner of **Lifestyle Correspondency** to construct a fresh community center in the heart of Port Augusta. The project, dubbed **Friends Circle Builds**, began in March and is slated for completion next month, providing residents with a versatile space for events, workshops, and social gatherings.

## What the Project Aims to Achieve

- **Reclaiming unused land** – The center is built on a former parking lot that had lain vacant for over a decade.

- **Promoting community cohesion** – Regular meetings, fitness classes, and art‑therapy sessions will be offered to all age groups.

- **Sustainable construction** – Green roofs, solar panels, and recycled building materials were selected to reduce the building’s carbon footprint.

> “We believe that when people come together, they can transform an ordinary piece of land into something extraordinary,” said **Megan Rhee**, Project Lead and local lifestyle columnist. “This is a tangible manifestation of our community’s spirit.”

## Key Milestones

- **March 2021** – Project launched and community rally held on Main Street.

- **February 2025** – Foundation laid; remote workers collaborated on design via livestream.

- **May 2025** – 80% of construction completed, with a soft opening scheduled for late July.

- **October 2025** – Official grand opening, attended by over 500 residents and local dignitaries.

## Community Involvement

The **Friends Circle Builds** initiative not only provided a physical space but also created numerous volunteer opportunities. 245 residents logged their hours on the construction site, and more than 30 local businesses donated materials or services.

### Success Stories

| Volunteer | Contribution | Comment |

|-----------|--------------|---------|

| Liam Patel | Masonry | “I never thought I’d get to use my skills for a real community project.” |

| Nia Cohen | Interior design | “Seeing the space come together was a gift.” |

| John Martinez | Scriptwriting | “I documented the project, and the footage is now part of the city’s history.” |

## Looking Ahead

The centre will host:

- **Weekly “Queer COVID‑Safe” tea‑times** for the LGBTQ+ community.

- **Monthly “Craft & Coffee” mornings** for local artisans.

- **Year‑round “Lifestyle Correspondency” seminars** that cover topics from mental health to eco‑friendly living.

The building’s opening will further foster the sense of belonging among Port Augusta’s diverse neighborhoods.

> “This is just the beginning,” noted city councilor **Aisha Rahman** during the opening ceremony. “With the Friends Circle Builds, we are nurturing a healthier, more connected Port Augusta.”

---

For more community updates and stories about local projects, visit the **[6_community](#6_community)** section of *The Port Augusta Times*.

headline: Yesterday’s Quick‑Warming Soccer Spotlight
content:
The residents of Port Augusta gathered yesterday in what will doubtless go on to become a beloved tradition; the town’s little senior soccer union turned their practice ground in Parliament Square *temporary community–warm‑up pitch*. Coaches and local citizens alike slipped past council banners at 1608 hrs ‒ and scored both good passes, warm cups of chilli, and unforgettable social cheer.

> *Link *Section 5 — Sports*

---

headline: Conventional Titan for Peace
content:
**Port Augusta Times**

*Port Augusta, 6 December 2025*

The city of Port Augusta has recently hosted a landmark event dubbed the **Conventional Titan for Peace** convention, bringing together environmental scientists, military strategists, and community leaders to explore how conventional (non‑nuclear) security measures can help prevent conflicts and foster sustainable development.

## A New Approach to Peacekeeping

At the heart of the convention was the discussion of large‑scale **conventional defence systems**—projectiles, drones, and barrier technologies—that, unlike their nuclear counterparts, carry a lower risk of escalation. The slogan “**Conventional Titan for Peace**” emphasised the dual role these systems can play: protecting communities from external threats while reducing the global appetite for nuclear armaments.

**“When we can rely on robust, low‑yield conventional forces, the diplomatic options widen dramatically,”** said Dr. Maya Clarke, a senior researcher at the Australian Defence Research School. **“It gives us a stepping stone to de‑militarise hotspots without compromising safety.”**

## Environmental Co‑Benefits

A key pillar of the convention was the environmental impact of deploying such systems. According to the **Department of Environment, Water, Heritage and the Arts**, conventional defence projects can be designed to minimise ecological footprints by:

- Using local materials to reduce carbon emissions during construction

- Partnering with renewable‑energy companies to power installations

- Implementing smart‑maintenance protocols to extend lifespan and reduce waste

These measures, the department said, align with the city’s larger goal of becoming a **carbon‑neutral hub by 2035**.

## Community‑Led Peace Initiatives

The convention also launched a series of **community‑led “Peace Pods”**—small, community‑managed defence platforms that can be activated in times of crisis. Each pod will be staffed and maintained by volunteers, offering a “human‑facilitated” approach to security that emphasises transparency and accountability.

**“We want peace not only to be a strategy on a charts of war,”** said council member James O’Neill. **“It must be a lived reality for our citizens.”**

## Looking Ahead

The convention concluded with a **Coalition for Conventional Peace** agreement, urging national governments to adopt a framework that prioritises conventional defense tools over nuclear arsenals. The coalition will meet again next year in Adelaide for a review of progress.

As Port Augusta celebrates its growing reputation as an environmental forward‑thinking city, the **Conventional Titan for Peace** initiative stands as a testament to the belief that peace and sustainability can—and must—go hand in hand.

*For further details, visit the city’s official website or contact the Department of Environment’s media office.*

headline: Suspect Senior Superintendent Paul Smith: A Growing Public‑Safety Concern
content:
**The Port Augusta Times** – *Public Safety Section (4_public_safety)*

In a developing story that has raised alarms across the region, Senior Superintendent Paul Smith of the Port Augusta Police Service has been named as a suspect in a series of questionable disciplinary actions and alleged misconduct. Investigators are now examining whether his actions may have compromised public safety, prompting a review of the department’s internal oversight procedures.

## Background

- **Position** – Senior Superintendent, Traffic & Community Safety Division

- **Tenure** – Over 12 years in the force, with 6 years as a superintendent

- **Reported Issues** – A series of officer complaints, unexplained disciplinary suspensions, and allegations of improper use of force

### Key Allegations

| Allegation | Details | Current Status |

|------------|---------|----------------|

| **Improper Use of Force** | Multiple reports of excessive force during traffic stops, some leading to injuries. | Investigations underway. |

| **Misallocation of Resources** | Accusations of diverting vehicles and personnel from high‑risk areas for personal use. | Police records cross‑checked; preliminary audit inconclusive. |

| **Failure to Report** | Reports of omitting 16 alleged infractions from official logs. | Police Superior Officers Council reviewing. |

## Impact on Public Safety

The Port Augusta Times has received numerous inquiries from residents concerned that:

- **Risk of Disaster Response** – Mismanagement of critical resources could delay emergency response times during natural or man‑made incidents.

- **Trust in Law Enforcement** – Public confidence in local policing ranks in decline.

- **Officer Morale** – Several junior officers have announced plans to transfer to neighboring districts citing a “turbulent environment.”

## Official Response

The Police Service Business, led by Chief Commissioner Jane Doe, has announced a *“comprehensive, independent review”* to determine the authenticity of the allegations:

1. **Internal Affairs Investigation Team** – Operating in collaboration with the Independent Police Integrity Authority (IPIA).

2. **Transparency Initiative** – Releasing anonymised data on patrol priorities and resource allocation to the public.

3. **Community Liaison** – Scheduling town‑hall meetings to discuss resident concerns and the findings of the investigation.

> **Chief Commissioner Jane Doe**: “Public safety is our foremost duty. We are committed to a thorough, unbiased review that upholds the integrity of our department.”

## What Residents Can Do

- **Report** – Any concerns or witnessed incidents can be filed through the official portaugusta.police.gov.au/complaints portal.

- **Attend Meetings** – The next public safety briefing is scheduled for 12 May 2025 at 7 p.m. in the Civic Hall, City Hall.

- **Stay Informed** – The Port Augusta Times will provide daily updates until the investigation concludes.

---

**Editor's Note:** This article is part of the *4_public_safety* coverage intended to keep the Port Augusta community informed. It remains a developing story; further details will be added as the investigation proceeds.

**HEADLINE:** *Local Pulse – Mayor Stuart Roberts — Navigating Growth While Keeping Community Values Front‑Front*

**By Samantha D’Arcy – 1_local_government Team**

**Port Augusta, AU, 27 September 2025**

---

The heart of Port Augusta’s governance has long been guided by an individual balancing progress with pride in the region’s cultural fabric. This month, the council and the city‑wide readership turn their focus on one figure at the helm: **Mayor Stuart Roberts**.

**Background & Rise**

> • Born and bred in Port Augusta, Stuart took over the mayoral office in 2021 following a council recall.

> • His prior years on the Planning and Services board championed eco‑friendly projects and community engagement.

> • Critics labelled the quick pivot between party platforms as a "crossover compromise".

**Policy Highlights**

1. **Sustainable Growth Agenda**

- “Port Augusta should keep rising while remembering what makes our corner the closest to Earth,” said Roberts.

- The 2022 Plan Green Boost subsidises community gardens, wildlife corridors, and mixed‑use developments.

2. **Port Enhancement for All**

- Miller Landing expansion improved storm‑water flooding tolerance *and* pedestrian lanes for commuters.

3. **Community Cohesion Initiatives**

- Year‑long "Stories at Sundown" programme launched to let town members recount lives that shaped neighbourhood identity.

**Controversies**

| Issue | What It Is | Mayor's Stance | Reaction |

|-------|------------|----------------|----------|

| The Harbor Lane | Contract renew‑al for maintenance crews | ‘Fair terms, timely execution.’ | Local businesses applauding improved schedules |

| Cultural Resource Conservation | Proposed shift in land‑use codes near old mill ruins | ‘Preserve but permit upgrades.’ | Archaeological Society issuing statement |

**Public Perception**

> *“We have this optimistic vibe that was missing before Stuart.”*

> — *May, 21 Atoise Resident, <1‑½ km north of river.*

**Community Testimonies**

- **Amira Al‑Jafari**, environmental NGO:  *“He introduced a real incentive for reforesting.”*

- **Leonardo Schmidt**, chief engineer of local power:  *“Reductions in carbon have translated into smaller utility bills.”*

**Personal Side**

Mayor Stuart is the type who plans “afternoons on the paddle‐board deck for Sunday family outing while sitting on a concrete wall about your ideas.”

**Quote from Mayor**

> *“The horizon can seem as wide as you want but to realize progress lies in each brick of small talk, community meal or a town debate where voices linger into the night.”*

> –  Stuart Roberts

**Upcoming Focus – 2026 Port Augusta Open Planning Summit**

- “Port Augusta values community values while pushing a *path to thrive.”* –  The Council.

- Address for youth representatives will be televised February next year at Miller Landing hall; RSVP needed.

### Contact Information

**Mayor Stuart Roberts**

Attn: City Planning & Development Office
